turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, just getting this screen up, it's crawling today. Grab a seat.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): No worries, I was a bit early. The telly out there was that loud I can't hear myself think.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yeah, it's rough. What brings you in?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Um, I wanted to sort out contraception. I've been going round in circles for weeks, reading forums at midnight, and I figured I'd just come and talk it through properly.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Contraception, right. Hang on, this has jumped to someone else's notes. Can you say that again?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): I want contraception. I was on the pill before and it really didn't agree with me, so I stopped, and now I need to pick something else.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Which one were you on?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Levlin, err, Levlen ED, the combined one, a hundred and fifty with thirty. I took one every day, and I stopped it back in March.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stopped in March. What was the problem with it?

[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): My head was absolutely pounding, like my skull was in a vice, nearly every afternoon. It started a couple of weeks after I began them, and I put up with it for months because I thought it'd settle.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, the pounding was while you were on the Levlen, not before?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Not before, no. Once I stopped, the headaches just disappeared, and they haven't come back at all.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any flashing lights, or zigzag lines, with those headaches?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing visual. No aura, if that's the word. Just the pain, and then it was gone.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain? Breathlessness?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain, and I'm not short of breath. I walk to the cafe for work and I'm fine on the hills, even when I'm running late.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke?

[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, I've overdone it a bit lately if I'm honest. Three or four cigarettes on a Friday night when I'm out, sometimes a Saturday, but I don't smoke through the week and I don't buy packs.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, three or four? I was clicking the wrong box.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, three or four, just Friday nights mostly. Not a daily thing, and some weeks none at all.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): The nurse has typed your medicines up. I've got sertaline, uh, sertraline, fifty milligrams. Is that what you take?

[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No, that's not right. I'm on a hundred milligrams of Zoloft, the sertraline, every morning for my anxiety, and she only caught the old dose because I was explaining how my Brisbane GP started me on fifty and then put it up.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): A hundred, not fifty. The field's locked, so I'll flag it and we won't pretend it's sorted today. Every morning, though?

[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Every morning, and I don't miss days. I've been on the hundred for about a year, which has helped the worry, though I still over-explain everything, as you can probably tell.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mm. Was there a mini pill as well, Noriday?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Someone wrote me a script for Noriday ages ago, but I never took it. I didn't even get to the chemist, so that one's a no.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Any medicine allergies?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No, none that I know of. I've had penicillin loads of times, for tonsillitis as a kid, and nothing happened, no rash or anything.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Family history of clots, or anything else I should factor in?

[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): My mum had a DVT in her thirties while she was on the pill. That's half of why I've been spiralling, because I keep picturing the same thing happening to me if I pick the wrong one.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Anything else from when you were on it?

[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): This might be nothing, but on the Levlen my feet felt dead by the end of a shift. Both of them went proper numb, not just achy, and I stand open till close in a cafe so I blamed the standing at first.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Say the feet again? I was half on the guideline page.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Both feet still go numb if I stand all day. It was worse on the pill, and it's milder now, but a double shift and my feet feel dead again.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any swelling in the legs? I'll have a look.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): No, no swelling. I check most nights because of Mum, and they're never puffy, just that dead numb feeling.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ankles are soft, no swelling there. Blood pressure is 122 over 78, pulse 74.

[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay, that number's better than I feel. I get wound up in here and afterwards I feel like a wet rag, properly wrung out, and that washed-out tiredness has been around for months, not just clinic days.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Tired for months. Periods, are they heavy, or painful?

[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Not heavy, and they're pretty regular. Day one is a bit crampy but nothing wild, I just use a heat pack. Sorry, I've got a frog in my throat, this is awkward, I'm not actually sick.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Bowels and bladder all behaving?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, all normal on that front. No diarrhoea or anything, and no stinging when I wee, I just wee more because I drink water all shift.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Given the headaches on Levlen, your mum's clot, and the smoking, I don't reckon we should put you back on a combined pill. It's the oestrogen I'd be worried about.

[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, I kind of knew you'd say that. I made a spreadsheet of the rod versus the hormonal IUD versus the copper one, which is embarrassing, but the irregular bleeding thing freaks me out.

[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): The implant, Implanon, goes in the arm and lasts three years, though the bleeding can be unpredictable. A hormonal IUD is very effective as well, and the copper one has no hormone if you'd rather that. Depo is a jab every twelve weeks, but you've never had that, have you?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Never had the injection, no. I don't like something I can't stop if the bleeding's awful. You can take the implant out, can't you?
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yeah, we can remove it if it's not suiting you. No script from me today. I'll give you the implant leaflet so you can read the bleeding bit properly before you decide.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): That'd help. Can the decision wait till next time, so I can read it and ask my sister? She had one, and I want the honest version, not the brochure version.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yep. Reception'll book you in two weeks, and you can tell me what you've decided. If you pick the implant, we'll arrange the insertion after that, not today.

[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks works, I've got a uni assignment before then. Do I need bloods, or is the blood pressure enough? And the sertraline really is a hundred, not the fifty, so I can bring the box if that helps.

[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Blood pressure's enough, no blood test today. The leaflet's yours, and please bring that box so we're not guessing. If you get chest pain, sudden breathlessness, or a headache that's different from those old ones, get seen straight away rather than waiting.

spec.situation: Young woman asks about contraception, previous pill caused headaches, smokes occasionally; blood pressure read; options discussed; implant leaflet given, decision next visit.

traps.happens: The patient describes things in colourful or sentence-like speech ('I've overdone it', 'I can't hear myself think', 'a frog in my throat', 'my feet feel dead', 'I feel like a wet rag').
traps.label_rule: Every symptom name is a short clinical noun phrase of 1 to 5 words ('voice fatigue', 'numbness in both feet', 'tiredness'), never a full sentence, never starting with I/we/my. Pure idioms that are not symptoms ('I can't hear myself think' said about classroom noise) are NOT symptoms. The patient's own words stay in the cited turn, not in the name.

features: disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.

stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats

bad.reason: Current bilateral foot numbness after standing is supported, but severity 'mild' is not stated.
bad.text: Numbness in both feet (category=neurological, status=present, severity=mild, frequency=after prolonged standing, temporality=current, body_site=both feet, aggravating_factors=prolonged standing, reported_by=patient, certainty=certain)

bad.reason: Counselling and options discussed are supported, but responsible_person should be doctor, not patient.
bad.text: Advised against restarting a combined oral contraceptive and discussed the implant, hormonal IUD, copper IUD and injection. (action_type=counselling, status=recommended, responsible_person=patient)

omissions.text: Current sertraline/Zoloft dose is 100 mg every morning; the recorded medication entry omits the 100 mg dose, and the patient said she does not miss doses and has been on 100 mg for about a year.
Levlen ED was stopped in March.
Headaches resolved completely after stopping Levlen and have not recurred.
Noriday was listed but the patient never took it and never filled the prescription.
The patient reported no medication allergies specifically and said she has tolerated penicillin previously without rash or reaction.
Maternal DVT occurred in her thirties and was while her mother was on the pill.
Both feet numbness was worse while on Levlen and is milder now, though it still occurs after standing all day.
Contraceptive preference/detail: patient is considering implant vs hormonal IUD vs copper IUD and is particularly concerned about irregular bleeding.
Negative finding: patient has never had the Depo injection.
Plan detail: no prescription was issued today.
Investigation plan: no blood tests are needed today; blood pressure alone is sufficient.
